CFDocument.creator: Alabama State Department of Education
CFDocument.title: World Languages (2017)
CFDocument.description:
Content standards in this document address Levels I-V for Grades 7-12 in world languages and Latin, and Levels I-IV for American Sign Language (ASL). Content standards for exploratory world languages programs for Grades K-8 are also included. The overlap for grade bands is included due to differences in local school configurations. These content standards are designed to help local school districts expand language programs within their districts. Program expansion may include Dual Language Programs, Foreign Language in Elementary Schools (FLES), Foreign Language Exploratory (FLEX) options, the College Board Advanced Placement Program, and the International Baccalaureate Program.
Content standards in the Alabama Course of Study: World Languages reflect the five goal areas of language learning as identified by the National Standards in Foreign Language Education Project in its 2015 national standards publication, World-Readiness Standards for Learning Languages, 4th Edition. These goals, Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons, and Communities, serve as the organizing principles of the World Languages document and resonate throughout the content standards in each grade level and content cluster. These standards are aligned to advance content across grade clusters and levels without recurrence of substance.

CFItems.fullStatement: World Languages
Novice Low Proficiency Range
Communication

Communicate on some very familiar topics using single words or learned phrases.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: likes/dislikes, sports, hobbies_

CFItems.fullStatement: Answer simple questions.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: What is your name? What day is today? What is the weather?_

CFItems.fullStatement: Connections

CFItems.fullStatement: Identify Latin influences on other disciplines.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Roman numerals, metric prefixes in (mathematics), anatomical terminology, and names of planets (science)._

CFItems.fullStatement: Identify evidence of contributions of Roman civilization and language to diverse cultures.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Architectural sites in Western Asia, North Africa, and Europe; and artistic interpretations of classical themes during the Renaissance._

CFItems.fullStatement: Comparisons
Recognize plots and themes of Greco-Roman myths and their influence in literature, art, and music.
Recognize Latin derivatives, cognates, and language patterns in English and other languages.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Mottoes, phrases, abbreviations, roots, prefixes, and suffixes._

CFItems.fullStatement: Communities
Identify similarities of their own culture to that of the Greco-Roman world.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Architecture, daily life, themes and heroes of classical mythology._

CFItems.fullStatement: Identify world languages and communities connected by their common origin in Latin language and Greco-Roman culture.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian._

CFItems.fullStatement: Identify professional fields that employ Latin terminology.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Medicine, law, pharmacy, engineering, and science._

CFItems.fullStatement: Level II
Communication
Interpersonal Mode
Ask and answer highly predictable and formulaic questions in Latin.
Answer simple questions using short Latin sentences.
Formulate simple questions and responses relevant to a reading or lesson.
Interpretive Mode
Read, understand, and translate Latin at an Intermediate Low level.
Summarize and translate passages of adapted or unadapted Latin appropriate to their level.
Answer questions in Latin or English to demonstrate understanding of adapted or unadapted Latin appropriate to their level.
CFItems.notes: _Examples of grammar and syntax appropriate to Level II: See the Latin Grammar Addendum._

CFItems.fullStatement: Presentational Mode
Produce Latin messages at a Novice Mid to Novice High Level.
Write short messages and notes in Latin on familiar topics.
Cultures
Explain the significance of people, events, social structures, and political terms in Roman history.
CFItems.notes:
_Examples: Heroes of the early Roman Republic, Scipio, Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar, Antony, Octavian, Constantine, and Justinian._

_Events include the founding of Rome, the secession of the Plebs, Punic Wars, and civil wars._

_Patrician and plebeian classes, the role of women in Roman society, and slavery in the ancient world._

_Monarchy, republic, populares, optimates, cursus honorum, First and Second Triumvirates._

CFItems.fullStatement: Compare the actions of Roman heroes and historical figures and explain the differences.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Compare the actions of Marius, Sulla, Caesar, or Cicero to Cincinnatus, Camillus, or Regulus._

CFItems.fullStatement: Connections
Locate historically significant cities, countries, and geographical features of the ancient Mediterranean world, and describe their relationship to their modern counterparts.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Carthage, Troy, Alexandria, Athens, Delphi, Constantinople; divisions of Gaul, Phoenicia, Magna Graecia, Crete, Sicily; Rubicon, Po, Nile, and Rhine rivers, the Alps and Pyrenees mountains._

CFItems.fullStatement: Investigate and describe Latin influences on modern academic disciplines, world languages such as English and the Romance languages, history, and philosophy.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Stoic and Epicurean philosophy on contemporary ideas and literature, similarities and differences between modern and Roman military tactics._

CFItems.fullStatement: Describe Roman influences on contemporary arts and culture.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: The television series_ Rome, _the movies_ Gladiator, Cleopatra, _and_ Troy, _and contemporary youth literature._

CFItems.fullStatement: Comparisons
Compare language patterns of Latin and their own language.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Differences in the way Latin and English express indirect statements._

CFItems.fullStatement: Use Latin prefixes, suffixes, and roots to expand English vocabulary.
Compare the geography and social, political, legal, military, and economic systems of the Roman world to systems of the modern world.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Compare a map of the provinces of the Roman Empire to a modern map of the Mediterranean region._

CFItems.fullStatement: Communities
Identify ways the study of Latin is beneficial to the study of other languages.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Similarities between the vocabulary of Latin and the Romance languages, as in the Latin word_ homo, _the Spanish word_ hombre, _and the French word_ l'homme.

CFItems.fullStatement: Connect with personal interests using knowledge of Latin and the Greco-Roman world.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Plan real or imaginary travel to places once a part of the Roman Empire, and listen to music, and sing songs in Latin._

CFItems.fullStatement: Level III
Communication
Interpersonal Mode

Answer simple questions using short, properly formulated Latin sentences.
Formulate questions and responses relevant to a reading or lesson using properly formulated Latin sentences.
Interact with others in formulaic social situations.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Carrying out more involved conversations in simple Latin sentences about a passage being read in class or conversing with others to learn more about them._

CFItems.fullStatement: Interpretive Mode
Read, understand, and translate Latin prose at an Intermediate Mid to Intermediate High level.
Demonstrate understanding of the main idea of paragraph-length Latin prose texts about familiar ideas.
Find information in Latin texts for practical purposes, including literary analysis.
Read, translate, and and demonstrate understanding of Latin texts that offer differing perspectives.
Analyze the style of Latin prose authors to comprehend content.
CFItems.notes:
_Examples: Describe the tone of a passage from Cicero_

_Explain the use of rhetorical devices in speeches by Cicero._

CFItems.fullStatement: Answer questions in Latin or English to demonstrate understanding of adapted or unadapted Latin prose authors appropriate to Level III.
CFItems.notes:
_Examples of grammar appropriate to Level III: See the Latin Grammar Addendum (Appendix A, page 67)._

_Examples of Latin prose authors: Caesar, Cicero, Pliny, Sallust, and Livy._

CFItems.fullStatement: Presentational Mode
Produce Latin sentences and phrases at a Novice High to Intermediate Low level.

CFItems.notes:
_Examples: Write sentences about topics of Roman and Greek culture and history._

_Prepare written materials for presentation, translating English sentences into Latin_

_Recite memorized authentic Latin prose such as Cicero's first Catilinarian oration._

CFItems.fullStatement: Cultures
Relate Roman cultural products to perspectives.
Investigate and describe values and perspectives in Roman prose authors.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Values of_ pietas _and_ gravitas _found in the writings of Pliny._

CFItems.fullStatement: Analyze important people in Roman history and literature to determine their cultural significance.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Gracchi brothers, Plautus, Terence, Cicero, Catiline, Sallust, Livy, Pliny the Elder, Pliny the Younger, Seneca, or Tacitus._

CFItems.fullStatement: Relate Roman cultural practices to perspectives.
Contrast the ideals of Roman political factions in the first Century B.C.E.
CFItems.notes: _Example: The conflict between Cicero and Catiline, the proposed policies of the_ optimates _and_ populares.

CFItems.fullStatement: Connections
Investigate the connections between Latin and other disciplines.
Describe and analyze the influence of themes in Roman prose on Western art and literature.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Jacque-Louis David's_ Oath of the Horatii.

CFItems.fullStatement: Access and evaluate information and diverse perspectives that originate from Latin and Roman culture.
Analyze figures from Roman history and literature to identify their influence on American history.
CFItems.notes: _Example: The influence of Cincinnatus on George Washington._

CFItems.fullStatement: Analyze the style of selections from Roman prose to investigate its influence on today's world of diverse cultures.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Phrases such as _"O tempora, O mores"_ in a modern context._

CFItems.fullStatement: Comparisons
Investigate, explain, and reflect on the nature of language through comparisons between Latin and their own language.
Compare the style of Roman prose authors to that used in contemporary history and politics.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Compare one of Pliny's letters to a current piece or writing, such as an open letter published in a newspaper._

CFItems.fullStatement: Analyze the structure of Roman rhetoric and its influence on contemporary rhetorical styles.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Compare one of Cicero's orations to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech._

CFItems.fullStatement: Investigate, explain, and reflect on the concept of culture through comparisons of the culture of the Greco-Roman world and their own.
Compare issues that reveal cultural similarities between the ancient world and modern cultures.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Sallust's account of the 63 B.C.E. senate debate on capital punishment and the modern debate on capital punishment, Cicero's consternation regarding the appropriate punishment of insurgent citizens and the current debate on what to do about domestic terrorism._

CFItems.fullStatement: Communities
Use knowledge of Latin and Greco-Roman culture in a multilingual world of diverse cultures.
Investigate important and influential works written in Latin.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Isaac Newton's_ Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica.

CFItems.fullStatement: Identify and correctly use English derivatives of Latin words commonly used in Latin prose.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Avarice, vulgar, suspicion, and perdition._

CFItems.fullStatement: Set goals and reflect on the progress made in using Latin for enjoyment, enrichment, and advancement.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Read Latin translations of literature at the appropriate proficiency level such as_ Ubi Fera Sunt (Where the Wild Things Are) _or_ Winnie Ille Pu (Winnie the Pooh).

CFItems.fullStatement: Level IV
Communication

CFItems.notes: _Example: Describe how the meter of a poem affects its meaning._

CFItems.notes: _Example: Dactylic hexameter in Vergil's_ Aeneid _--"Ārmă vĭ/rūmqŭe că/nō Trō/iāe quī/prīmŭs ăb/ōrīs" (DDSSDS)._

CFItems.notes:

_Examples: Vergil, Ovid, Horace, and Catullus._

CFItems.fullStatement: Presentational Mode
Produce Latin sentences and phrases at an Intermediate Low level.

CFItems.fullStatement: Read or recite from memory authentic Latin poetry with proper inflection and attention to meter.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Catullus' 5_ ("Vivamus, mea Lesbia, atque amemus"), _Horace's_ Odes _1.11_ ("Carpe Diem")

CFItems.fullStatement: Cultures
Relate Roman cultural products to perspectives.
Explain the significance of Roman poets and their poetry.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Vergil, Horace, Ovid, Catullus, Martial, the patron Maecenas._

CFItems.fullStatement: Investigate, explain, and reflect on the relationship between Roman cultural practices and perspectives.
Compare the actions and character traits of figures in Roman poetry to actions and character traits of figures in other periods of history and literature.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Vergil's Aeneas and George Washington, Ovid's Daedalus and Leonardo da Vinci._

CFItems.fullStatement: Analyze Roman values and perspectives in poetry.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Critique Horace's use of Epicurean and Stoic philosophies._

CFItems.fullStatement: Connections
Analyze and critique Roman poetry to determine its influence on art and literature throughout history.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Ovid's influence on Gianlorenzo Bernini's sculptural rendition of_ Daphne and Apollo, _William Shakespeare's_ Romeo and Juliet, _and Leonard Bernstein's_ West Side Story.

CFItems.fullStatement: Describe the influence of themes in Roman poetry on Western art and literature.
CFItems.notes: _Example: The theme of artistic discipline and loss in Ovid's tale of Orpheus and Eurydice as interpreted in film and opera._

CFItems.fullStatement: Comparisons
Compare phrases used in English to their origins in Latin literature.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: "vanish into thin air," "hair stands on end," and "voice sticks in your throat" originating in Vergil's_ Aeneid.

CFItems.fullStatement: Connect universal themes found in Roman poetry to artistic renditions of other time periods and cultures.
CFItems.notes: _Example: Themes of love and hate in different versions of Catullus' 85_ "Odi at amo" _and works by English poets Abraham Cowley (1667), Ezra Pound (1972), and Garry Wills (contemporary)._

CFItems.fullStatement: Communities
Investigate connections between the study of Latin around the world and across time to the present.
CFItems.notes: _Example: The study of Latin in European schools, and Milton's Latin works._

CFItems.fullStatement: Apply Latin vocabulary commonly used in poetry to understand English derivatives.
CFItems.notes: _Examples: Urbane, amorous, incantation, and Occident._
